title: Give a Little, Get a Little Mindful Manager, November 8, 2026
author: Sara Royo
source: The Art of Asking Questions (theartofaskingquestions.com), guest post by Sara Royo of The
summary: Sara Royo, writing as a guest in Andrea Chiarelli's newsletter, starts from the familiar joke about earning brownie points and uses it to explain how trust is actually built at work. She argues that cynical, visible favour banking backfires because nobody wants to feel managed, while genuine help given with nothing expected tends to come back around. Drawing on Gouldner's norm of reciprocity and Nowak and Sigmund's indirect reciprocity, she shows that small acts of help build a reputation that reaches people you never helped directly. She then maps how trust building changes across a career: juniors earn it through reliability and usefulness, mid-career people through sharing knowledge and contacts, and senior people by giving away power, credit and opportunity. The closing claim is that goodwill built early means you rarely have to ask for favours later.
points: Cynical favour banking is easy to spot and erodes trust; help works only when it is given without a hidden negotiation behind it.
Reciprocity is slow and uncounted, and indirect reciprocity means a reputation for helping benefits you from people you never helped.
Early in a career reliability beats brilliance: do what you said you would do, take the unglamorous task, and notice colleagues who are struggling.
Mid-career trust comes from generosity with knowledge and introductions, and hoarding what you know makes people trust you less.
Senior trust is built by giving credit, opening doors, and keeping your word or protecting your team when it is inconvenient.
quotes: Reciprocity in a healthy relationship isn’t the crude “I did you a favour, so now you owe me” of the brownie points joke. It’s slower and less conscious than that.
What builds up over a run of interactions like these isn’t a debt to be settled but an expectation that we’ll be there for each other, which is a rather different and more durable thing.

In practice, helping people builds a reputation for being someone worth cooperating with, and that reputation makes others more inclined to cooperate with you in turn, including people you have never done anything for directly.
When you’re junior, reliability is worth more than brilliance, and it’s almost entirely within your control.

This is the stage where hoarding becomes a temptation, but it’s a big mistake. It can feel safer to be the only person who understands a system or knows the right contact, but the people who guard their knowledge tend to be trusted less because others can sense the calculation behind it.
You don’t become less impressive because someone else is recognised; quite the opposite, you become the kind of leader people want to work for.
And people notice whether you keep your word when it turns out to be inconvenient, or whether you protect your team when something goes wrong or start looking for someone to blame.
Build the relationships long before you need anything from them, and mostly you’ll find you never have to ask.
